sections.title: Topic 107: Introduction to Generative Models
sections.body:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import torchvision
import torchvision.transforms as transforms
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import linalg

print("="*80)
print("GENERATIVE MODELS: CREATING NEW DATA")
print("="*80)

print("""
🎨 WHAT ARE GENERATIVE MODELS?

Discriminative Models (Classification):
   Learn: P(y|x) - "Given input x, what is class y?"
   Example: Is this image a cat or dog?

Generative Models:
   Learn: P(x) or P(x|y) - "What does data x look like?"
   Example: Generate new cat images!

Key Capabilities:
   ✅ Generate new samples
   ✅ Understand data distribution
   ✅ Data augmentation
   ✅ Unsupervised/semi-supervised learning
   ✅ Compression
   ✅ Anomaly detection

📊 TYPES OF GENERATIVE MODELS:

1️⃣  GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks):
   • Two networks compete: Generator vs Discriminator
   • Game theory approach
   • High-quality images
   • Training can be unstable

2️⃣  VAEs (Variational Autoencoders):
   • Encoder-decoder with probabilistic latent space
   • Smooth interpolation
   • Stable training
   • Sometimes blurry outputs

3️⃣  Diffusion Models:
   • Iterative denoising process
   • State-of-the-art quality (DALL-E 2, Stable Diffusion)
   • Slower generation
   • Very stable training

4️⃣  Autoregressive Models:
   • Generate one element at a time
   • GPT, PixelCNN
   • High quality but slow

5️⃣  Flow-Based Models:
   • Invertible transformations
   • Exact likelihood
   • RealNVP, Glow

🎯 APPLICATIONS:

Art & Creativity:
   • Image generation (DALL-E, Midjourney)
   • Style transfer
   • Super-resolution
   • Image-to-image translation

Science:
   • Drug discovery (molecule generation)
   • Protein design
   • Data augmentation

Entertainment:
   • Deepfakes
   • Game content
   • Video synthesis

Text:
   • Text generation (GPT)
   • Machine translation
   • Dialogue systems
""")

# Visualize the generative model landscape
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 12))

# GAN
ax = axes[0, 0]
ax.text(0.5, 0.7, 'GAN', fontsize=20, fontweight='bold', ha='center')
ax.text(0.5, 0.5, 'Generator ⚔️ Discriminator', fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(0.5, 0.3, '✅ High quality\n❌ Training instability', fontsize=10, ha='center')
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis('off')
ax.set_facecolor('#ffe6e6')

# VAE
ax = axes[0, 1]
ax.text(0.5, 0.7, 'VAE', fontsize=20, fontweight='bold', ha='center')
ax.text(0.5, 0.5, 'Encoder → Latent → Decoder', fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(0.5, 0.3, '✅ Stable training\n❌ Blurry outputs', fontsize=10, ha='center')
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis('off')
ax.set_facecolor('#e6f3ff')

# Diffusion
ax = axes[1, 0]
ax.text(0.5, 0.7, 'Diffusion', fontsize=20, fontweight='bold', ha='center')
ax.text(0.5, 0.5, 'Iterative Denoising', fontsize=12, ha='center')
ax.text(0.5, 0.3, '✅ SOTA quality\n❌ Slow generation', fontsize=10, ha='center')
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.axis('off')
ax.set_facecolor('#e6ffe6')

# Comparison
ax = axes[1, 1]
models = ['GAN', 'VAE', 'Diffusion']
quality = [9, 6, 10]
speed = [8, 9, 4]
stability = [5, 9, 9]

x = np.arange(len(models))
width = 0.25

ax.bar(x - width, quality, width, label='Quality', color='#ff6b6b')
ax.bar(x, speed, width, label='Speed', color='#4ecdc4')
ax.bar(x + width, stability, width, label='Stability', color='#95e1d3')

ax.set_ylabel('Score (1-10)', fontweight='bold')
ax.set_title('Generative Models Comparison', fontweight='bold', fontsize=14)
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(models)
ax.legend()
ax.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('generative_models_overview.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\n✅ Saved: generative_models_overview.png")
plt.close()
```

sections.title: Topic 108: GANs - Generative Adversarial Networks
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- THE GAN GAME (Goodfellow et al., 2014)
- Simple GAN Generator for MNIST.
- Simple GAN Discriminator for MNIST.
- Single training step for GAN.
- Generator tries to fool discriminator

**Defines:** `Generator`, `Discriminator`, `train_gan_step()`

```python
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("GANs: GENERATIVE ADVERSARIAL NETWORKS")
print("="*80)

print("""
🎮 THE GAN GAME (Goodfellow et al., 2014)

Two Neural Networks in Competition:

1. Generator (G):
   • Input: Random noise z ~ N(0, 1)
   • Output: Fake image G(z)
   • Goal: Fool the discriminator

2. Discriminator (D):
   • Input: Real or fake image
   • Output: Probability [0, 1] (real?)
   • Goal: Distinguish real from fake

Training Process:
   1. Sample real images from dataset
   2. Generate fake images: G(z)
   3. Train D to classify real vs fake
   4. Train G to fool D
   5. Repeat!

Analogy:
   • Generator = Counterfeiter (makes fake money)
   • Discriminator = Police (detects fake money)
   • Both get better over time!

Mathematical Formulation:
   min_G max_D V(D,G) = 𝔼[log D(x)] + 𝔼[log(1 - D(G(z)))]
   
   D maximizes: Correctly classify real (D(x)→1) and fake (D(G(z))→0)
   G minimizes: Make fakes look real (D(G(z))→1)

Optimal Solution:
   When training converges: D(x) = 0.5 everywhere
   → Discriminator can't tell real from fake!
""")

class Generator(nn.Module):
    """
    Simple GAN Generator for MNIST.
    
    Architecture:
        z (100) → FC → FC → FC → Image (784)
    """
    
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=100, img_size=784):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 256),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(256),
            
            nn.Linear(256, 512),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(512),
            
            nn.Linear(512, 1024),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(1024),
            
            nn.Linear(1024, img_size),
            nn.Tanh()  # Output in [-1, 1]
        )
    
    def forward(self, z):
        img = self.model(z)
        return img

class Discriminator(nn.Module):
    """
    Simple GAN Discriminator for MNIST.
    
    Architecture:
        Image (784) → FC → FC → FC → Probability (1)
    """
    
    def __init__(self, img_size=784):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(img_size, 512),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),
            
            nn.Linear(512, 256),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),
            
            nn.Linear(256, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()  # Output probability
        )
    
    def forward(self, img):
        validity = self.model(img)
        return validity

# Initialize models
latent_dim = 100
img_size = 28 * 28

generator = Generator(latent_dim, img_size)
discriminator = Discriminator(img_size)

print(f"\nGAN Architecture:")
print(f"Generator parameters:     {sum(p.numel() for p in generator.parameters()):,}")
print(f"Discriminator parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in discriminator.parameters()):,}")

# Training step demonstration
def train_gan_step(real_imgs, generator, discriminator, g_optimizer, d_optimizer):
    """Single training step for GAN."""
    
    batch_size = real_imgs.size(0)
    
    # Adversarial ground truths
    real_labels = torch.ones(batch_size, 1)
    fake_labels = torch.zeros(batch_size, 1)
    
    # ---------------------
    #  Train Discriminator
    # ---------------------
    d_optimizer.zero_grad()
    
    # Real images
    real_loss = F.binary_cross_entropy(discriminator(real_imgs), real_labels)
    
    # Fake images
    z = torch.randn(batch_size, latent_dim)
    fake_imgs = generator(z)
    fake_loss = F.binary_cross_entropy(discriminator(fake_imgs.detach()), fake_labels)
    
    # Total discriminator loss
    d_loss = (real_loss + fake_loss) / 2
    d_loss.backward()
    d_optimizer.step()
    
    # -----------------
    #  Train Generator
    # -----------------
    g_optimizer.zero_grad()
    
    # Generate fake images
    z = torch.randn(batch_size, latent_dim)
    fake_imgs = generator(z)
    
    # Generator tries to fool discriminator
    g_loss = F.binary_cross_entropy(discriminator(fake_imgs), real_labels)
    g_loss.backward()
    g_optimizer.step()
    
    return d_loss.item(), g_loss.item()

print("""
GAN Training Tips:
   ✅ Use LeakyReLU (not ReLU) in discriminator
   ✅ Use BatchNorm in generator
   ✅ Label smoothing (0.9 instead of 1.0 for real)
   ✅ Train D more than G initially
   ✅ Use Adam optimizer (lr=0.0002, betas=(0.5, 0.999))
   ✅ Monitor both losses

Common Problems:
   ❌ Mode collapse: G produces limited variety
   ❌ Vanishing gradients: G loss → 0
   ❌ Oscillation: Neither converges
   ❌ Training instability
""")
```

diagrams.title: GANs, VAEs and diffusion models
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TB
  gan["GAN: generator makes fakes, discriminator spots them — trained against each other"]
  vae["VAE: encoder → latent distribution → decoder; sample the latent space to generate"]
  dif["Diffusion: learn to remove noise step by step; start from pure noise to generate"]
  gan --> use["Sharp images, unstable training"]
  vae --> use2["Smooth latent space, blurrier samples"]
  dif --> use3["State-of-the-art quality, slower sampling"]
diagrams.explain: All three learn to generate new data. GANs are a two-player game that produces sharp samples but can be unstable; VAEs learn a smooth latent space; diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual noising process and power most modern image generators.

sections.title: Topic 109: Advanced GANs
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- GAN EVOLUTION:
- DCGAN Generator for 64×64 images.
- DCGAN Discriminator for 64×64 images.
- GAN Best Practices:

**Defines:** `DCGANGenerator`, `DCGANDiscriminator`

```python
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("ADVANCED GAN ARCHITECTURES")
print("="*80)

print("""
🚀 GAN EVOLUTION:

1️⃣  DCGAN (2016): Deep Convolutional GAN
   • Convolutional architecture
   • Use strided convs (no pooling)
   • BatchNorm in generator
   • Guidelines for stable training

2️⃣  WGAN (2017): Wasserstein GAN
   • Different loss function (Wasserstein distance)
   • More stable training
   • Meaningful loss metric
   • Weight clipping

3️⃣  WGAN-GP (2017): WGAN with Gradient Penalty
   • Gradient penalty instead of weight clipping
   • Even more stable
   • Better convergence

4️⃣  StyleGAN (2019): Style-Based Generator
   • Control over different scales
   • Mixing styles
   • State-of-the-art faces
   • 1024×1024 resolution

5️⃣  StyleGAN2 (2020): Improved Architecture
   • Better quality
   • Fewer artifacts
   • Path length regularization

6️⃣  BigGAN (2019): Large Scale GAN
   • 512×512 ImageNet
   • Class-conditional generation
   • Orthogonal regularization

📊 CONDITIONAL GANs (cGAN):

Idea: Control what is generated
   • Input: noise z + label y
   • Output: Image of class y

Applications:
   • Text-to-image (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion)
   • Image-to-image translation (pix2pix)
   • Super-resolution

🎨 CycleGAN: Unpaired Image Translation

Problem: Translate images without paired data
   • Horse → Zebra
   • Summer → Winter
   • Photo → Painting

Solution: Cycle consistency
   X → G(X) → F(G(X)) ≈ X
   
   Losses:
   1. Adversarial (fool discriminators)
   2. Cycle consistency (X → Y → X)
   3. Identity (preserve colors)
""")

class DCGANGenerator(nn.Module):
    """
    DCGAN Generator for 64×64 images.
    
    Architecture: Progressive upsampling with transposed convolutions.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, latent_dim=100, channels=3):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.init_size = 4
        self.l1 = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 512 * self.init_size ** 2)
        )
        
        self.conv_blocks = nn.Sequential(
            nn.BatchNorm2d(512),
            
            # 4×4 → 8×8
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),
            nn.Conv2d(512, 256, 3, stride=1, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(256),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            
            # 8×8 → 16×16
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),
            nn.Conv2d(256, 128, 3, stride=1, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(128),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            
            # 16×16 → 32×32
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),
            nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 3, stride=1, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.LeakyReLU(0.2),
            
            # 32×32 → 64×64
            nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2),
            nn.Conv2d(64, channels, 3, stride=1, padding=1),
            nn.Tanh()
        )
    
    def forward(self, z):
        out = self.l1(z)
        out = out.view(out.shape[0], 512, self.init_size, self.init_size)
        img = self.conv_blocks(out)
        return img

class DCGANDiscriminator(nn.Module):
    """
    DCGAN Discriminator for 64×64 images.
    
    Architecture: Strided convolutions for downsampling.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, channels=3):
        super().__init__()
        
        def discriminator_block(in_filters, out_filters, bn=True):
            block = [
                nn.Conv2d(in_filters, out_filters, 4, 2, 1),
                nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True),
                nn.Dropout2d(0.25)
            ]
            if bn:
                block.append(nn.BatchNorm2d(out_filters))
            return block
        
        self.model = nn.Sequential(
            *discriminator_block(channels, 64, bn=False),  # 64×64 → 32×32
            *discriminator_block(64, 128),                  # 32×32 → 16×16
            *discriminator_block(128, 256),                 # 16×16 → 8×8
            *discriminator_block(256, 512),                 # 8×8 → 4×4
        )
        
        # Final layer
        self.adv_layer = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(512 * 4 * 4, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )
    
    def forward(self, img):
        out = self.model(img)
        out = out.view(out.shape[0], -1)
        validity = self.adv_layer(out)
        return validity

dcgan_gen = DCGANGenerator()
dcgan_disc = DCGANDiscriminator()

print(f"\nDCGAN Architecture:")
print(f"Generator params:     {sum(p.numel() for p in dcgan_gen.parameters()):,}")
print(f"Discriminator params: {sum(p.numel() for p in dcgan_disc.parameters()):,}")

# Test forward pass
z = torch.randn(4, 100)
fake_imgs = dcgan_gen(z)
print(f"\nGenerated image shape: {fake_imgs.shape}")  # (4, 3, 64, 64)

print("""
✅ GAN Best Practices:

Architecture:
   • Use strided convs (not pooling)
   • BatchNorm in generator
   • LeakyReLU everywhere
   • Tanh in generator output
   • No fully connected layers (except first/last)

Training:
   • Learning rate: 0.0002
   • Adam optimizer: betas=(0.5, 0.999)
   • Batch size: 64-128
   • Label smoothing: 0.9 for real
   • One-sided label smoothing

Monitoring:
   • Visual inspection (most important!)
   • Inception Score (IS)
   • Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)
   • Generator and discriminator losses
""")
```

sections.title: Topic 110: VAEs - Variational Autoencoders
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- THE VAE APPROACH (Kingma & Welling, 2013)
- Variational Autoencoder for MNIST.
- Encode input to latent parameters.
- Reparameterization trick: z = μ + σ * ε
- Reconstruction loss (binary cross-entropy)
- KL divergence: -0.5 * Σ(1 + log(σ²) - μ² - σ²)

**Defines:** `VAE`, `vae_loss()`

```python
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("VAEs: VARIATIONAL AUTOENCODERS")
print("="*80)

print("""
🧬 THE VAE APPROACH (Kingma & Welling, 2013)

Architecture:
   Input → [Encoder] → Latent (μ, σ) → [Decoder] → Reconstruction

Key Idea: Probabilistic latent space
   • Encoder: q(z|x) - probability of z given x
   • Decoder: p(x|z) - probability of x given z
   • Latent z ~ N(μ, σ²) - Normal distribution

Reparameterization Trick:
   Instead of: z ~ N(μ, σ²)
   Use: z = μ + σ · ε, where ε ~ N(0, 1)
   
   Why? Allows backpropagation through sampling!

Loss Function:
   L = Reconstruction Loss + KL Divergence
   
   1. Reconstruction: ||x - x̂||²
      → How well can we reconstruct input?
   
   2. KL Divergence: D_KL(q(z|x) || p(z))
      → How different is q(z|x) from N(0,1)?

KL Divergence (closed form for Gaussians):
   D_KL = -0.5 * Σ(1 + log(σ²) - μ² - σ²)

Benefits:
   ✅ Smooth latent space (interpolation!)
   ✅ Stable training
   ✅ Explicit likelihood
   ✅ Can do semi-supervised learning

Limitations:
   ❌ Blurry reconstructions
   ❌ Lower quality than GANs
   ❌ Posterior collapse
""")

class VAE(nn.Module):
    """
    Variational Autoencoder for MNIST.
    
    Architecture:
        Encoder: 784 → 400 → 20 (μ, σ)
        Decoder: 20 → 400 → 784
    """
    
    def __init__(self, input_dim=784, hidden_dim=400, latent_dim=20):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Encoder
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.fc_mu = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        self.fc_logvar = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        
        # Decoder
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(latent_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.fc4 = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, input_dim)
    
    def encode(self, x):
        """
        Encode input to latent parameters.
        
        Returns:
            mu: Mean of latent distribution
            logvar: Log variance of latent distribution
        """
        h = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        mu = self.fc_mu(h)
        logvar = self.fc_logvar(h)
        return mu, logvar
    
    def reparameterize(self, mu, logvar):
        """
        Reparameterization trick: z = μ + σ * ε
        
        Args:
            mu: Mean
            logvar: Log variance
        
        Returns:
            z: Sampled latent vector
        """
        std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)
        eps = torch.randn_like(std)
        z = mu + eps * std
        return z
    
    def decode(self, z):
        """
        Decode latent vector to reconstruction.
        """
        h = F.relu(self.fc3(z))
        reconstruction = torch.sigmoid(self.fc4(h))
        return reconstruction
    
    def forward(self, x):
        """
        Forward pass: encode → reparameterize → decode
        """
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = self.reparameterize(mu, logvar)
        reconstruction = self.decode(z)
        return reconstruction, mu, logvar

def vae_loss(reconstruction, x, mu, logvar):
    """
    VAE loss = Reconstruction + KL Divergence
    
    Args:
        reconstruction: Reconstructed input
        x: Original input
        mu: Mean of latent distribution
        logvar: Log variance of latent distribution
    
    Returns:
        loss: Total VAE loss
    """
    # Reconstruction loss (binary cross-entropy)
    BCE = F.binary_cross_entropy(reconstruction, x, reduction='sum')
    
    # KL divergence: -0.5 * Σ(1 + log(σ²) - μ² - σ²)
    KLD = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp())
    
    return BCE + KLD

# Initialize VAE
vae = VAE(input_dim=784, hidden_dim=400, latent_dim=20)

print(f"\nVAE Architecture:")
print(f"Input dimension:  784 (28×28)")
print(f"Hidden dimension: 400")
print(f"Latent dimension: 20")
print(f"Total parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in vae.parameters()):,}")

# Example forward pass
x = torch.randn(32, 784)
reconstruction, mu, logvar = vae(x)
loss = vae_loss(reconstruction, x, mu, logvar)

print(f"\nExample forward pass:")
print(f"Input shape:          {x.shape}")
print(f"Reconstruction shape: {reconstruction.shape}")
print(f"Latent μ shape:       {mu.shape}")
print(f"Latent logvar shape:  {logvar.shape}")
print(f"Loss:                 {loss.item():.2f}")

print("""
✅ VAE Applications:

1. Image Generation:
   • Sample z ~ N(0,1)
   • Decode to image

2. Image Interpolation:
   • Encode two images → z₁, z₂
   • Interpolate: z = α·z₁ + (1-α)·z₂
   • Decode interpolated z

3. Data Compression:
   • Encode to low-dimensional z
   • Lossy compression

4. Anomaly Detection:
   • High reconstruction error = anomaly

5. Semi-Supervised Learning:
   • Use latent space for classification
""")
```

sections.title: Topic 111: Diffusion Models
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- DIFFUSION MODELS (Ho et al., 2020)
- Simplified Diffusion Model (noise prediction).
- Args: x: Noisy image (batch, channels, H, W) t: Timestep (batch, 1)
- Cosine schedule for beta (variance schedule).

**Defines:** `SimpleDiffusion`, `cosine_beta_schedule()`

```python
print("\n" + "="*80)
print("DIFFUSION MODELS: STATE-OF-THE-ART GENERATION")
print("="*80)

print("""
🌊 DIFFUSION MODELS (Ho et al., 2020)

The Big Idea:
   • Forward process: Gradually add noise to data
   • Reverse process: Learn to denoise

Forward Diffusion (Fixed):
   x₀ → x₁ → x₂ → ... → xₜ → ... → x_T
   
   Add Gaussian noise at each step:
   q(xₜ|xₜ₋₁) = N(xₜ; √(1-βₜ)·xₜ₋₁, βₜ·I)
   
   After T steps: x_T ≈ N(0, I) (pure noise)

Reverse Diffusion (Learned):
   x_T → xₜ → ... → x₁ → x₀
   
   Learn: p(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) = N(xₜ₋₁; μ_θ(xₜ,t), Σ_θ(xₜ,t))
   
   Neural network predicts noise to remove!

Training:
   1. Sample real data x₀
   2. Sample timestep t ~ Uniform(1, T)
   3. Sample noise ε ~ N(0, I)
   4. Create noisy version: xₜ = √(ᾱₜ)·x₀ + √(1-ᾱₜ)·ε
   5. Predict noise: ε̂ = model(xₜ, t)
   6. Loss: ||ε - ε̂||²

Generation:
   1. Start with pure noise x_T ~ N(0, I)
   2. For t = T to 1:
      • Predict noise ε̂ = model(xₜ, t)
      • Denoise: xₜ₋₁ = remove ε̂ from xₜ
   3. Return x₀ (generated image)

Why Diffusion Models Win:
   ✅ State-of-the-art quality
   ✅ Stable training (no adversarial)
   ✅ Flexible (can condition on text, etc.)
   ✅ Mathematical foundation
   ✅ Gradual refinement

Challenges:
   ❌ Slow generation (T=1000 steps!)
   ❌ High memory usage
   → Solutions: DDIM (faster sampling), latent diffusion
""")

class SimpleDiffusion(nn.Module):
    """
    Simplified Diffusion Model (noise prediction).
    
    For demonstration - real models are much larger!
    """
    
    def __init__(self, img_channels=3, time_embed_dim=128):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Time embedding
        self.time_embed = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1, time_embed_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(time_embed_dim, time_embed_dim)
        )
        
        # Simplified U-Net structure
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(img_channels, 64, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )
        
        self.middle = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(128 + time_embed_dim, 128, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )
        
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(64, img_channels, 3, padding=1),
        )
    
    def forward(self, x, t):
        """
        Args:
            x: Noisy image (batch, channels, H, W)
            t: Timestep (batch, 1)
        
        Returns:
            Predicted noise
        """
        # Time embedding
        t_emb = self.time_embed(t)  # (batch, time_embed_dim)
        t_emb = t_emb.view(t_emb.shape[0], -1, 1, 1)
        t_emb = t_emb.repeat(1, 1, x.shape[2], x.shape[3])
        
        # Encoder
        h = self.encoder(x)
        
        # Add time embedding
        h = torch.cat([h, t_emb], dim=1)
        
        # Middle
        h = self.middle(h)
        
        # Decoder
        noise_pred = self.decoder(h)
        
        return noise_pred

def cosine_beta_schedule(timesteps, s=0.008):
    """
    Cosine schedule for beta (variance schedule).
    
    Better than linear schedule for image generation.
    """
    steps = timesteps + 1
    x = torch.linspace(0, timesteps, steps)
    alphas_cumprod = torch.cos(((x / timesteps) + s) / (1 + s) * torch.pi * 0.5) ** 2
    alphas_cumprod = alphas_cumprod / alphas_cumprod[0]
    betas = 1 - (alphas_cumprod[1:] / alphas_cumprod[:-1])
    return torch.clip(betas, 0.0001, 0.9999)

# Example
model = SimpleDiffusion()
timesteps = 1000
betas = cosine_beta_schedule(timesteps)

print(f"\nDiffusion Model:")
print(f"Parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}")
print(f"Timesteps: {timesteps}")

# Forward pass
x = torch.randn(4, 3, 32, 32)  # Batch of images
t = torch.randint(0, timesteps, (4, 1)).float()
noise_pred = model(x, t)

print(f"\nExample forward pass:")
print(f"Input shape:         {x.shape}")
print(f"Timestep shape:      {t.shape}")
print(f"Predicted noise:     {noise_pred.shape}")

# Visualize beta schedule
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(betas.numpy())
plt.xlabel('Timestep', fontweight='bold')
plt.ylabel('β_t', fontweight='bold')
plt.title('Noise Schedule (Cosine)', fontweight='bold', fontsize=14)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
alphas = 1 - betas
alphas_cumprod = torch.cumprod(alphas, dim=0)
plt.plot(alphas_cumprod.numpy())
plt.xlabel('Timestep', fontweight='bold')
plt.ylabel('ᾱ_t (cumulative product)', fontweight='bold')
plt.title('Signal Decay Over Time', fontweight='bold', fontsize=14)
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('diffusion_schedule.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
print("\n✅ Saved: diffusion_schedule.png")
plt.close()

print("""
Famous Diffusion Models:

1. DALL-E 2 (OpenAI, 2022):
   • Text-to-image generation
   • 1024×1024 images
   • CLIP guidance

2. Stable Diffusion (Stability AI, 2022):
   • Open-source text-to-image
   • Latent diffusion (operates in latent space)
   • Efficient (can run on consumer GPUs)

3. Imagen (Google, 2022):
   • Text-to-image
   • Photorealistic images
   • Cascade architecture

4. Midjourney:
   • Commercial service
   • Artistic images
   • Discord-based
""")
```

sections.body:
```python
print("GENERATIVE MODELS: APPLICATIONS & EVALUATION")
```

🎨 REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS:

1. Image Synthesis:
- DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion
- Generate from text descriptions
- Art, design, prototyping

2. Image Editing:
- Inpainting (fill missing regions)
- Outpainting (extend image)
- Style transfer
- Super-resolution

3. Face Generation & Editing:
- StyleGAN for realistic faces
- Age progression/regression
- Attribute editing (smile, hair color)

4. Data Augmentation:
- Generate training data
- Improve model robustness
- Balance datasets

5. Drug Discovery:
- Generate molecular structures
- Optimize drug properties
- Faster R&D

6. 3D Generation:
- Text-to-3D models
- DreamFusion, Point-E
- Game assets, metaverse

7. Video Generation:
- Animate images
- Generate short clips
- Video editing

📊 EVALUATION METRICS:

**1. Inception Score (IS):**
Formula: exp(𝔼[D_KL(p(y|x) || p(y))])

**Measures:**
- Quality: Clear class labels
- Diversity: Variety of classes

Range: Higher is better
Problem: Doesn't compare to real data!

**2. Fréchet Inception Distance (FID):**
Formula: ||μ_real - μ_fake||² + Tr(Σ_real + Σ_fake - 2√(Σ_real·Σ_fake))

**Measures:**
- Distance between real and fake distributions
- Uses Inception network features

Range: Lower is better (0 = identical)
Gold standard for image generation!

**3. Precision & Recall:**
- Precision: Are generated images realistic?
- Recall: Does generator cover full distribution?

Trade-off: High precision may mean low diversity

**4. Perceptual Path Length (PPL):**
- Smoothness of latent space
- Lower = smoother interpolations
- Used for StyleGAN

**5. Human Evaluation:**
- Ultimate metric!
- A/B testing
- User studies

```python
def calculate_fid(real_features, fake_features):
    """
    Calculate Fréchet Inception Distance.
    
    Args:
        real_features: Features from real images (N, D)
        fake_features: Features from fake images (M, D)
    
    Returns:
        fid: FID score (lower is better)
    """
    # Calculate mean and covariance
    mu_real = np.mean(real_features, axis=0)
    mu_fake = np.mean(fake_features, axis=0)
    
    sigma_real = np.cov(real_features, rowvar=False)
    sigma_fake = np.cov(fake_features, rowvar=False)
    
    # Calculate FID
    diff = mu_real - mu_fake
    
    # Product might be complex with small negative eigenvalues
    covmean, _ = linalg.sqrtm(sigma_real @ sigma_fake, disp=False)
    if np.iscomplexobj(covmean):
        covmean = covmean.real
    
    fid = diff @ diff + np.trace(sigma_real + sigma_fake - 2 * covmean)
    
    return fid

# Example FID calculation (with dummy data)
real_features = np.random.randn(1000, 2048)
fake_features = np.random.randn(1000, 2048)

fid_score = calculate_fid(real_features, fake_features)
print(f"\nExample FID Score: {fid_score:.2f}")
print("(Lower is better; 0 = identical distributions)")
```

🎯 MODEL SELECTION GUIDE:

**Choose GAN when:**
✅ Need highest quality images
✅ Have expertise in GAN training
✅ Speed is important (after training)
✅ Don't need exact likelihood

**Choose VAE when:**
✅ Need stable training
✅ Want smooth latent space
✅ Need compression
✅ Want exact likelihood
✅ Doing semi-supervised learning

**Choose Diffusion when:**
✅ Want state-of-the-art quality
✅ Training stability is priority
✅ Have compute for slow generation
✅ Need conditional generation (text-to-image)
✅ Can use latent diffusion for efficiency

⚠️ ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS:

❌ Deepfakes: Misinformation, impersonation
❌ Bias: Models reflect dataset biases
❌ Copyright: Training on copyrighted data
❌ Misuse: Fake IDs, synthetic data abuse
❌ Environmental: High compute = carbon footprint

✅ Responsible Use:
- Watermark generated content
- Disclosure (AI-generated)
- Bias testing and mitigation
- Respect copyright
- Consider environmental impact

sections.title: Summary: Generative Models
sections.body:
### Three Main Approaches

```
1. GANs (Adversarial)
   Generator ⚔️ Discriminator
   • High quality
   • Training instability
   • No explicit likelihood

2. VAEs (Probabilistic)
   Encoder → Latent → Decoder
   • Stable training
   • Smooth latent space
   • Sometimes blurry

3. Diffusion (Iterative Denoising)
   Noise → ... → Image
   • SOTA quality
   • Slow generation
   • Very stable
```

### Key Models Timeline

```
2014: GAN (Goodfellow)
2013: VAE (Kingma & Welling)
2016: DCGAN (Radford)
2017: WGAN-GP
2019: StyleGAN, BigGAN
2020: DDPM (Ho)
2022: DALL-E 2, Stable Diffusion, Imagen
```

### Evaluation Metrics

| Metric | What It Measures | Better |
|--------|------------------|--------|
| **FID** | Distribution distance | Lower |
| **IS** | Quality & diversity | Higher |
| **PPL** | Latent smoothness | Lower |
| **Human** | Actual perception | Preference |
